title: Urban Green Spaces
summary: A city's small park experiment reveals what a map of green space can miss.
paragraphs: From a distance, the city of Fenbridge appears well supplied with parks. On the municipal map, a broad riverside reserve makes almost a fifth of the central district look green. Yet the streets behind its northern boundary had few trees, and residents there told planners that a short walk on a hot afternoon could be uncomfortable. The reserve was visible through a fence, but the two public gates both opened onto the southern road. On paper, many homes lay within three hundred metres of green space. On foot, reaching it could require a long detour. The council began to ask whether it was counting land when it should also have been counting journeys.

A trial in the northern district used two former parking areas rather than extending the reserve. One became a small garden with trees, benches and a drinking fountain. The other kept its open surface and received chairs beneath a temporary canopy. The council wanted to compare places that offered immediate shelter with places where shade would increase as trees matured. On summer afternoons, researchers recorded which seats people used and measured conditions at sitting height. They also counted people passing the sites, because a busy route could bring more visitors even if the new space itself was no more attractive than its quieter counterpart.

At the garden, the shallow layer of new soil dried quickly, and several young trees lost leaves during a dry spell. The canopy site had no such difficulty and drew more visitors in the first summer. That early result did not settle the question of what to build elsewhere. On one street, an established tree gave shade over part of the pavement long before people reached a seat. Its leaves also released water vapour, a process that can contribute to local cooling when water is available. The researchers therefore distinguished conditions around a mature tree from the benefits that residents could expect during the first years of a planting project.

The trial also showed the limitations of a single midday count. The small garden looked quiet at the hottest hour but became a meeting place after nearby classes ended. Some people used the shaded seats for long conversations; others stopped for barely a minute on their way to the bus. The canopy, close to a busy crossing, was used more often for brief rests. Neither pattern was inherently more valuable. To understand who benefited, the team combined observations at different times of day with short interviews. A space designed around only the busiest hour would have overlooked some of the people for whom a place to pause mattered most.

As the council considered further sites, it asked its maintenance staff to review each proposal before construction. In some streets, pipes limited the depth available for roots. In others, a narrow pavement would leave too little room for wheelchairs if planters were placed beside every bench. Staff suggested larger shared planting beds where they could maintain a continuous volume of soil. They also wanted young trees to have a reliable water supply. These concerns changed the budget: the council reserved money for watering and care after opening, even though those costs were less visible to the public than the planting ceremony.

Fenbridge eventually published two maps. The first still showed the amount of green land in each district. The second followed likely walking routes and marked places where shade or seats were available, together with barriers such as closed gates. The new map did not declare that the best sites had already been found. Instead, it directed planners to routes where a small change could help people get to school, a shop or a bus stop. They could then visit the route with local users before deciding whether to add a bench, plant a tree or improve access to a park that already existed.

questions.prompt: Both public gates of the riverside reserve faced the southern road.
questions.quote: the two public gates both opened onto the southern road
questions.explanation: The passage locates both gates on that road, which explains the detour from the north.

questions.prompt: The northern trial increased the size of the riverside reserve.
questions.quote: A trial in the northern district used two former parking areas rather than extending the reserve.
questions.explanation: The trial reused parking areas instead of adding land to the reserve.

questions.prompt: The temporary canopy was brought from a sports facility.
questions.quote: The other kept its open surface and received chairs beneath a temporary canopy.
questions.explanation: The passage describes where the canopy was installed but gives no information about its previous location.

questions.prompt: The canopy site attracted fewer visitors than the garden in the first summer.
questions.quote: The canopy site had no such difficulty and drew more visitors in the first summer.
questions.explanation: The passage reports the opposite comparison: the canopy site drew more visitors.

questions.prompt: The garden became a meeting place after classes finished nearby.
questions.quote: The small garden looked quiet at the hottest hour but became a meeting place after nearby classes ended.
questions.explanation: The later use of the garden followed the end of the nearby classes.

questions.prompt: The council bought its young trees from a nursery within Fenbridge.
questions.quote: They also wanted young trees to have a reliable water supply.
questions.explanation: The article discusses keeping young trees watered but never identifies a supplier or its location.

questions.prompt: What problem did the council identify with its original map?
options: The green area of the reserve was measured incorrectly.
Straight-line proximity could disguise a difficult walking route.
The map confused public parks with private gardens.
The map placed the reserve outside the central district.
questions.quote: On paper, many homes lay within three hundred metres of green space. On foot, reaching it could require a long detour.
questions.explanation: Distance on the map did not describe the journey that residents could actually make.

questions.prompt: Why did researchers count people passing the two trial sites?
options: To decide when to close each site for maintenance.
To calculate the number of seats required by law.
To find out whether trips to the main park had declined.
To account for differences in how busy the routes already were.
questions.quote: a busy route could bring more visitors even if the new space itself was no more attractive
questions.explanation: Existing foot traffic could explain higher visitor numbers without indicating that the design was better.

questions.prompt: Why does the author mention an established tree?
options: To illustrate benefits that young plantings would not deliver immediately.
To explain why readers should disregard measurements at sitting height.
To show that mature trees never need water.
To suggest that the garden should replace every temporary canopy.
questions.quote: The researchers therefore distinguished conditions around a mature tree from the benefits that residents could expect during the first years of a planting project
questions.explanation: The established tree illustrates what developed shade can provide, in contrast with the early years of a new planting.

questions.prompt: Which conclusion did the team draw about observing only at midday?
options: Midday observations are sufficient on days without classes.
Brief stops should be excluded from visitor counts.
A single observation period can miss significant uses of a space.
People prefer long conversations beside busy crossings.
questions.quote: A space designed around only the busiest hour would have overlooked some of the people for whom a place to pause mattered most.
questions.explanation: Observations made at one time would have missed how and when some residents used the location.

questions.prompt: What change was made to the budget after maintenance staff reviewed the plans?
options: The council stopped funding any permanent planting.
The council set aside funding for care after the spaces opened.
The council restricted spending to streets without underground pipes.
The council moved all funds from benches to wheelchair ramps.
questions.quote: the council reserved money for watering and care after opening
questions.explanation: The change was to provide continuing maintenance funding after construction.

questions.prompt: What was the intended role of the second map?
options: To confirm a final ranking of every possible park site.
To replace visits and discussions with local residents.
To show only the shortest routes to the riverside reserve.
To identify routes where planners could investigate practical improvements.
questions.quote: it directed planners to routes where a small change could help people get to school, a shop or a bus stop
questions.explanation: The map helped planners choose routes to investigate before deciding what should change.
